reason: Broken on the edition, not on the poet. The evidence names “Bells and Pomegranates No. VII: Dramatic Romances and Lyrics, Edward Moxon, 1845”, and the card would print “Dramatic Romances and Lyrics (1845)”. I fetched the Wikisource index behind that transcription: the scan is Page:Bells And Pomegranates Second Series (IA in.ernet.dli.2015.123086).pdf, and its index reads Publisher “Ward, Lock & Company, Ltd.”, Address London, Year 1897, Editor Thomas James Wise. So the wording was never checked against the 1845 Moxon printing named on the card. It was checked against an 1897 reprint edited by Thomas J. Wise, the bibliographer later exposed as a forger and manipulator of Victorian texts, and there is no Moxon 1845 scan in the Internet Archive listing for this title (every accessible copy is the Ward, Lock reissue of 1896 to 1897). The distinctive readings ride on that one book. Searching the Wikisource Page namespace for “wakes in England” returns the Wise reprint alone with “And who wakes in England” and “brush-wood sheaf”; every other scan-backed edition reads “And whoever wakes in England” and “brushwood”, including one printed in Browning’s lifetime: Once a Week vol. 8 (1863), the Oxford Book of English Verse 1250 to 1900 (no. 729, checked in the raw page transcription), the 1918 Oxford Book, The Hundred Best Poems (lyrical) second series ed. Adam L. Gowans 1904 (pages 45 and 46, a proofread transcription), and Hoyt’s Cyclopedia 1922. Two outcomes are possible and I cannot separate them from here: the Wise volume is a faithful type-facsimile and “who wakes” is the 1845 setting Browning later revised, or the reprint drifted. Either way the card as it stands fails this track’s rule, because it dates a reading to an edition nobody opened, and it carries an empty note, so a reader who knows the poem meets “who wakes” as an apparent typo with nothing to explain it. Everything else about the line is sound and should survive the fix: attribution right, section I right for 1845 (in that printing II is the Nelson stanza later moved to Nationality in Drinks and III is “Nobly Cape Saint Vincent”, later Home-Thoughts, from the Sea), no speaker needed, in scope, publishable, squarely on April, verse lineation and head capitals correct, source 105 characters with no dash. shipped.js: not shipped, nothing near, Browning 0 of 3, not banned, and he appears once in the month. The fix is one of two: ship the received text, “Oh, to be in England / Now that April’s there, / And whoever wakes in England / Sees, some morning, unaware, / That the lowest boughs and the brushwood sheaf / …”, naming a text actually seen (the Gowans 1904 page is proofread and reads “OH, to be in England” with “whoever” and “brushwood”; the Oxford Book reads “O to be in England”, so its wording is not interchangeable); or keep the facsimile reading and add a note that says plainly it is the 1845 text as reprinted by Wise for Ward, Lock in 1897 and that every later edition reads “whoever”. What must not ship is the present pairing of the rare reading with a bare 1845 date and no note.
